articles.title_orig: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.title_zh: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Russian hybrid attacks could cause a mass-casualty event in Europe, a report has warned, as Moscow steps up sabotage operations across the continent.
The study, carried out by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), found that sabotage operations across the continent had risen by 16 per cent and focused on countries that supported Kyiv.
Poland suffered 24 per cent of all the attacks while Germany faced 20 per cent and the Baltic states – including Latvia , Estonia and Lithuania – faced 20 per cent.
Instances of violent attacks have also increased significantly, with a rise in arson attacks and the use of improvised explosive devices (IEDs).
Russian proxies have demonstrated increased capabilities with more complex IEDs deploying timed and remote detonators.
It comes as Europe has faced cyberattacks across supermarkets, blood banks and airports.
“Sabotage has not yet achieved a strategic effect, but a mass-casualty incident is possible as the space for miscalculation narrows,” the report said.
“A single operation that caused fatalities or prolonged disruption would generate demands for retaliation and likely expose divisions between European governments.”
It predicted that European governments would be likely to continue responding to Russia ’s attacks “one incident at a time”.
“Despite recent attacks and attempted attacks in Estonia, Lithuania and Romania, none has set out red lines, with concern about escalation the primary instinct,” it continued.
It warned: “The effect is that the first mass-casualty attack (deliberate or by miscalculation) would set the terms of Europe’s response, with governments acting under pressure and possibly divided.”
This approach has done little to impact the Kremlin’s strategy and the report offered suggestions on how to improve the chances of changing the Kremlin’s approach.
“Publicly signalling, at least among Nato member states, what level of harm triggers which response would give Europe a better chance of changing the Kremlin’s calculation,” it said.
The study assessed attacks between October 2025 and September 2026.
The fallout from the war has spread beyond Europe too, with a Russian warship sunk in Benghazi, Libya following a Ukrainian attack.
The explosion took place on board Merkury, a Russian navy warship docked at the Benghazi naval base.
Satellite images by Vantor showed the ship was a Russian Navy corvette, or small warship, with pictures showing that most of the vessel had capsized and sunk, with only its bow still visible above water while smoke rises.
It came a day after Finland’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, warned that the Russia-Ukraine conflict was “spilling over” after a Russian ship was reportedly on fire in Finnish waters last Saturday.

articles.title_orig: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
articles.title_zh: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
articles.content_orig:
Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday.
The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not  provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact.
“The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” according to an Air Force spokesperson.
Reuters first reported about this most recent cyber intrusion against federal assets.
The FBI’s National Crime Information Center — which is used by federal, state and local authorities to share important information — was recently breached, sources briefed on the matter told NBC News this week .
And about two months ago, the FBI and Dutch national police arrested leaders of a “global cybercrime and threat actor group” that alleged stole employee information from a bureau database. It is unclear whether any of these breaches are related.
“We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities. Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said Friday.
“The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements. Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Gordon Lubold is a national security reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Trump Downplays China and Russia's Support to Iran
articles.title_zh: Trump Downplays China and Russia's Support to Iran
articles.content_orig:
Trump Downplays China and Russia's Support to Iran
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran, amid reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target US military bases.
Trump, during a short press conference with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida on Thursday, noted that the Iran conflict had been discussed during his recent trilateral meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
"My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they're very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information," AFP quoted Trump as saying.
"We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too," he added.
Regarding Russia's intelligence sharing, Trump said "I don't think they give very much."
He said both countries want to see the conflict with Iran end, and "I think they're helping me in that regard."
French Far-left Leader Demands 'Overhaul' of German Ties
French hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon on Friday called for an "overhaul" of ties with Berlin, voicing stinging criticism of Germany's economic dominance in the EU and its record military spending.
The France Unbowed (LFI) party leader, who is polling in second place for April's election, told French broadcaster LCI during a Berlin visit that he sees a "need for a thorough overhaul of the French-German relationship".
"I am hostile to the liberal (economic) policy of German governments that dominates the European Union," the 75-year-old said ahead of the launch of the German edition of his latest book at Berlin's Babylon cinema.
Melenchon’s economic platform, which includes a proposal to cancel French debt held by the European Central Bank, is dramatically opposed to traditional German doctrines of tight budgets and low borrowing.
Melenchon -- currently the favorite to reach a run-off against far-right veteran Marine Le Pen -- has also railed against Chancellor Friedrich Merz's commitment to transform the German military into the "strongest conventional army in Europe".
"We have the duty to ask: to make war against whom?" he said Friday, warning that Paris could be drawn into unwanted conflict as Germany's growing military strength makes it a "target" for other countries.
Melenchon’s rivals have accused him of cozying up to President Vladimir Putin's Russia, with LFI's pledge to leave NATO a particular concern for many of France's allies amid the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The far-left party leader has been highly critical of Germany's position in the conflict, accusing Merz's government of saber-rattling.
"They need to tone it down, because all this one-upmanship leads nowhere," he said.
But Melenchon flatly denied charges he is "Germanophobic," calling himself a "sort of disciple of Karl Marx" and a lover of Beethoven.
He also expressed pride at the German translation of his latest book, published in English under the title "Now, the People! Revolution in the 21st Century".
The politician further touted his close ties with Germany's far-left Die Linke party, which finished first in Berlin's state election in September.
Melenchon met the party's national leader Ines Schwerdtner on Friday, saying the two were "united in mobilizing against an economy of rearmament and war".
Mossad and Israeli Military Chiefs at Odds Over Striking Iran
Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman and military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir are at odds over whether to launch another strike against Iran. While Gofman supports a unilateral Israeli attack without US participation if no alternative remains, Zamir favors waiting for a decision from US President Donald Trump.
Israeli news website Ynet, in a report published jointly with Yedioth Ahronoth on Friday, said Gofman had adopted a more hawkish position during recent security discussions, amid concerns that Iran may be secretly continuing to develop chemical weapons.
According to senior officials familiar with his position, Gofman believes further delays in confronting the alleged Iranian chemical weapons threat could leave Israel facing an operational challenge that would be far more difficult to eliminate.
In Gofman's assessment, the mere emergence of such a threat makes it too risky to allow Iran to acquire these capabilities.
Security sources said Mossad and Israeli military intelligence, known as Aman, share the same intelligence assessments. Zamir also supports striking Iran but believes the threat is not yet imminent.
Zamir considers it preferable to await Trump's decision and act alongside the Americans, whose participation could provide a significant force multiplier and improve the chances of achieving a lasting strategic outcome.
A security source said the military's position is that Israel would attack without US involvement if an immediate existential threat emerged.
"But that is not the situation at present," the source added.
Reuters reported on November 18, citing two informed sources, that the Israeli military assesses Iran does not pose an imminent threat to Israel, meaning immediate military action is unnecessary.
Ynet explained that operational responsibility for any strike would ultimately fall to the Israeli military. The air force would carry out the main offensive operations, air defenses would respond to Iranian retaliation, and military intelligence would provide the information needed to sustain the campaign.
Disagreement Before the Elections
The differences between Gofman and Zamir date back to before Israel's elections.
According to Ynet, Trump raised military readiness for a possible strike against Iran roughly a month before the elections, prompting Israel to reach its highest level of alert.
Zamir opposed going to war before the elections, while Gofman took a different position, arguing that Israel should seize the opportunity to act jointly while the United States remained prepared to participate.
Trump ultimately abandoned plans for the attack, and the alert level was lowered.
Gofman visited Washington three weeks ago, presenting new intelligence concerning developments in Iran's alleged chemical weapons program and seeking to advance plans for a joint strike. His position was based on the assessment that the opportunity to inflict significant damage on Iranian capabilities would not remain open indefinitely.
Two sources told Reuters that Gofman had advocated joint US-Israeli strikes during meetings with American officials and had met CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
They said Gofman briefed US officials on Israeli intelligence concerning Iran, with one source indicating that the information related to Tehran's nuclear program.
Israeli media also reported that Gofman traveled to Miami to meet US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Former Israeli minister Ron Dermer, a close associate of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was in the United States around the same time to advocate a joint attack, according to the two sources.
The sources described Gofman's and Dermer's contacts as part of Netanyahu's efforts to persuade Trump to launch another strike against Iran, saying Netanyahu believes the opportunity is narrowing.
One source said Israel fears the United States could begin withdrawing its substantial military deployment from the region before the end of the year.
Following the visit, Trump announced on November 9 that he was postponing strikes against Iran after meeting Qatar's prime minister.
A source involved in diplomatic efforts said Gulf leaders had urged Trump not to attack Tehran.
Washington has yet to make a decision.
Ynet said the window of opportunity being discussed in Israel extends until the new US Congress is sworn in, approximately six weeks away.

articles.title_orig: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.title_zh: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

articles.title_orig: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.title_zh: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.content_orig:
Cybersecurity threats escalate as Leah Siskind analyzes Google’s warning about hackers using AI to automate cyberattacks against companies. Discussing the battle between defenders and attackers with John Roberts, the FDD AI Research fellow references Anthropic’s release of advanced models months ago. Siskin warns that super advanced AI models now have the dangerous ‘ability to detect vulnerabilities’ in software systems.
Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant ?
An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans.
We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
Google's Gemini assistant can retrieve information from connected Gmail accounts to answer questions, raising concerns about how private emails may be handled. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts . The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers.
In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process.
Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents.
In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback.
The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services.
Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see.
We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy:
"Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features."
Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files.
Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures . In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model.
On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment.
However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. We asked Google whether people who previously connected their accounts were notified about the updated disclosures or asked to provide additional consent. Google's response did not directly address those questions. Instead, the company emphasized that the newer connections are optional and can be disabled. articles.title_orig: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.title_zh: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.content_orig:
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

articles.title_orig: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
articles.title_zh: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
articles.content_orig:
Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.
Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.
"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.
It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.
"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution,"  Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said.
"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added.
The company has cancelled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued.
Norse was founded in March 2021 and offered cheap flights between Europe, the U.S., North America, Africa, and Asia.
The U.S.-Iran war began on Feb. 28 and caused jet fuel prices to skyrocket, forcing airlines around the world to grapple with higher costs. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor .
Norse Atlantic's Roald told CNBC in May that he wasn't "overly concerned," about access to fuel but flagged that the company had canceled over 700 flights, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers.
Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary warned in April that if jet fuel prices continued to stay elevated throughout the year, then other European airlines were likely to face "financial difficulties" during the winter season.
In fact, several European airlines have stopped operating this winter, including Slovakia's AirExplore, Spain's AlbaStar, Ireland's Fly4, and Spain's Plus Ultra, which has canceled all flights but hasn't permanently closed.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
articles.title_zh: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
articles.content_orig:
Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump.
It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era.
The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País ' s final polling averages . A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO.
It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year.
Despite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises.
Inflation soared to 4.9% in the year to October, above a euro zone average of 4%. November's flash estimate published Friday showed Spanish inflation cooling to 4.1%, still well above the 2.3% reading at the start of the year. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing one of the country's two most important issues.
Home purchase prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat . In 2025, house prices rose nearly three times as fast as household incomes, the European Commission said.
Nationwide protests began after an 87-year-old woman died two weeks after being evicted from her Madrid apartment in September.
Sánchez called the snap election after lawmakers rejected two government decrees designed to broaden housing protections, including limiting rent increases and blocking certain evictions and automatic lease renewals. Congress later ratified a revised version of one decree, limiting rent increases and evictions in some circumstances.
Sánchez has made a name for himself internationally after clashing with Trump over NATO spending, the war in Gaza and Spain's refusal to let U.S. forces use its bases for operations against Iran. Trump even threatened to cut off "all trade" with Spain during the dispute over the bases.
At a Nov. 21 rally in Tenerife, Sánchez asked: "What good has President Trump brought to the United States and, by extension, to the world?"
He has also told voters that the PP and Vox would roll back government cost-of-living assistance. Days before the election, Sánchez's government approved 1.21 billion euros ($1.33 billion) to extend public transport discounts through 2027 and approved a general pay increase of up to 4.5% for 2027.
But in a final pre-election survey for El Español on Nov. 23, 66% of respondents gave Sánchez a failing grade and 29.5% a passing one. His government has faced scrutiny over its handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis, two deadly train collisions this year and corruption cases involving people close to the prime minister.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the current favorite to replace Sánchez, has made alleged government corruption and inflation central to his campaign. At a Nov. 22 rally in Murcia, he said the government wanted voters to forget "that inflation is eating into your pay check, that you can't afford a home, that you're paying more than ever for everything."
The PP led the final El País polling average, published Nov. 24, with 31.4%, followed by Sánchez's Socialists at 29.1% and Vox at 17.9%. Several seat projections put the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. If Vox joins a government, it would be the first far-right party to do so since Spain returned to democracy after Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled for 40 years, died in 1975.
The PP wants to repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in designated high-pressure areas. It proposes speeding up construction permits and lowering taxes on first homes for buyers under 40. Vox also wants to repeal the housing law and would prioritize Spanish citizens for subsidized housing and public services.
Sánchez's Socialists want to extend renter protections and make at least a quarter of new homes public or permanently price-restricted. It would use proceeds from a bank levy to support housing, which it says will raise a further $1.5 billion. The PP has pledged to scrap this.
The PP also favors easing climate rules, extending the life of nuclear plants and replacing a decree that sets tight new renewable-power requirements on data centers with large new grid connections.
A PP-Vox coalition would have its tensions, with immigration likely to be a major pressure point as Vox has an increasingly hard line on deportation and the militarization of some borders. The parties clashed in regional governments over the distribution of unaccompanied migrant children, leading Vox to quit several coalitions in 2024.
Immigration has since gained more prominence amid the government's handling of reports that more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31.
"Immigration has played a significant role in supporting Spain's recent growth, a strong role for Vox could complicate the government's ability to sustain that," said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
The parties also differ on defense commitments: both support more investment, but neither has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defense. The PP pledges closer NATO cooperation, while Vox puts greater emphasis on border security.
The PP favors closer integration with the European Union, while Vox wants more independence from it. The success or failure of a PP-Vox partnership will also have wider lessons for Europe "where long-standing firewalls against far-right parties are coming under strain," added Middleton, pointing to the rise of Germany's AfD and the prospect of Marine Le Pen potentially winning next year's election in France.
A shift to the right could improve relations between the U.S. and Spain. Sánchez used his tenure to strengthen ties with Beijing, the country's largest goods trading partner outside the EU.
The U.S. remained Spain's largest source of foreign direct investment. Flows more than doubled to 11.6 billion euros in the 12 months through June 2026, from 5.1 billion euros in the previous 12 months, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Carla Hobbs, head of the European Council on Foreign Relations' Madrid office, expects a PP-led government to seek closer ties with Washington and bring its China policy more in line with the EU's. Vox could complicate that. The first test for Washington would be whether a new government changes Spain's position on defense spending or the use of its bases.

articles.title_orig: North Korea halts Russia military aid over Seoul row, Kyiv says
articles.title_zh: North Korea halts Russia military aid over Seoul row, Kyiv says
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has suspended military assistance to Russia following a diplomatic dispute over Moscow's statements on Seoul, Ukraine's military intelligence directorate said on Wednesday, in claims neither Moscow nor Pyongyang has confirmed or denied.
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) said North Korean leader Kim Jong-un personally made the decision after Pyongyang took offence at remarks by Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko, who said in October that the Kremlin would help de-escalate tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
North Korea's Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui characterised the statements as "not consistent with the spirit of the allied agreements between the two states" and announced a temporary suspension of military support, the HUR said.
The suspension includes a ban on Russian military transport aircraft using North Korean airspace, a halt to deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and a stop to further artillery munitions shipments, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
North Korea is also holding back from fulfilling a Russian request to expand its military contingent on Russian territory from 8,500 to 50,000 troops, the HUR added.
Rudenko made no public statement in those terms, but told Russian state media on 20 October that Moscow was ready for a "normalisation of relations" with Seoul.
"We do not link our relations with any country to what is happening with Ukraine. Therefore, if our South Korean partners take any practical steps, then of course they will be welcomed on our part," he said.
On 16 November, a senior aide to Kim, Politburo Presidium member Cho Yong Won, met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, on the eve of the APEC summit.
Moscow and Pyongyang had made no official statements in response to the HUR report at the time of publication.
Putin and Kim signed a mutual defence pact in June 2024, after which North Korea became one of Russia's closest military partners in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine. Russia deployed North Korean troops in an offensive later that year against Ukrainian forces in the Russian border region of Kursk.
Russia remains heavily dependent on North Korean weapons and materiel. In exchange, Pyongyang is understood to be seeking military technology, raw materials and financial assistance, as well as operational experience from Russia's war in Ukraine.
North Korea's army numbers more than 1 million personnel, making it one of the largest in the world.

articles.title_orig: Allstate Joins Growing List of Companies Hit by Tech Outages
articles.title_zh: Allstate Joins Growing List of Companies Hit by Tech Outages
articles.content_orig:
Allstate has joined the growing list of companies bedeviled by a technology disruption in recent weeks, leaving some customers unable to file claims or seek roadside assistance during Thanksgiving week.
The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages.
"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims," the company said. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."
People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday.
In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone.
Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks , software providers and government agencies.
Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said.
"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

articles.title_orig: Pregnant inmate escapes custody during Whataburger stop in New Mexico
articles.title_zh: Pregnant inmate escapes custody during Whataburger stop in New Mexico
articles.content_orig:
A pregnant prisoner is on the run in New Mexico after escaping in a corrections department SUV following a prenatal doctor appointment on Wednesday.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, who was not restrained at the time because of her pregnancy, managed to slide into the front seat of the Dodge Journey transport vehicle and drive away as she was returning to Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants from the appointment in Albuquerque, according to the corrections department.
Taylor escaped while the correctional officers accompanying her had stopped at a Whataburger, according to The Associated Press.
The Dodge Journey was later located via GPS, but Taylor was no longer in the vehicle, corrections officials said. Her prison jumpsuit was found near the vehicle, the AP reported.
Taylor is serving time after pleading guilty to four offenses related to the theft of a vehicle, vehicle burglary and receiving a stolen car, according to court records.
She is from Cleveland, Texas, which is located outside of Houston, where she also has ties, according to authorities. Officials said they were following up on leads she may have taken public transportation and were checking Greyhound buses and Amtrak trains.
Taylor is about 5-foot-7 and 180 pounds and has blue eyes and red hair. Authorities are asking anyone who sees her to call 911.
All prison facilities in New Mexico were put on lockdown in the wake of the escape as a precaution. That lockdown was lifted at 6 a.m. on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Trump claims revised economic data shows pre-midterms figures were ‘fake’ | First Thing
articles.title_zh: Trump claims revised economic data shows pre-midterms figures were ‘fake’ | First Thing
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."
Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate . That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.
That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post , suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections , where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and multiple governorships.
"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.
However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.
On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.
The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.
Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary . Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. That data is later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.
GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five-year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.
The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.
Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.
Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."
"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.
Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool . They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: No warning, no mercy: why China moved fast to topple Chen Jining
articles.title_zh: No warning, no mercy: why China moved fast to topple Chen Jining
articles.content_orig:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.
The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.
He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.
“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”
Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.
Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.
Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.
“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.
The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.
“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.
“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.
The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.
Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography .
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring .
The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest , a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.
The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.
Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.
“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.
Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
Max Burman is deputy editor in the London bureau of NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow
articles.title_zh: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from October's record highs.
The market correction, defined as a 10% decline from a recent high, came as investor concern mounted over a potential slowdown in AI spending, mega-cap tech valuations and the path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Nov. 20 alone, closing at 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive daily decline. That left the index 11.6% below the Oct. 6 closing high of 7,818.93.
A correction can deepen into a bear market, defined as a drop of 20% or more from the most recent top. But history shows that even a bear market, let alone a correction, doesn't automatically mean the economy is destined for a recession.
In a CNBC analysis, eight of the 13 S&P 500 bear markets overlapped with recessions, as defined by the National Bureau of Economic Research, and five did not. The NBER says a recession is "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months."
The 1973-74 oil shock, the dot-com bust in 2000, the 2007-09 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic downturn all overlapped with recessions. But some major bear markets also occurred without one, including in 1987 and 2022.
Deutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen said that every S&P 500 bear market since the 1962 "Kennedy Slide" has coincided with at least one of three factors: a recession, worsening economic data raising recession fears, or a cycle of Federal Reserve rate hikes. None of those are present today, at least so far.
"Much as last week's selloff was severe, it's worth remembering that it has several differences with many of the other big risk-off moves in recent times," the London-based strategist wrote on Tuesday.
Allen said there hasn't been any sudden reassessment of the growth outlook recently, which happened during the Covid-19 shock, when the pandemic pushed the global economy into recession and the S&P 500 plunged 33.9% in just 33 days. Nor is the current situation similar to the 2025 "Liberation Day" tariff period either, which also prompted a reassessment of the growth outlook.
Economic numbers aren't deteriorating either, with the November U.S. flash composite Purchasing Managers' Index, or PMI, at 54.6, above 50 and indicating that business activity continued to expand. Another factor that often coincides with a recession, Allen said, was a big hawkish shift from the central banks, seen in the 1966 and 2022 bear markets.
"Today however, the equity declines have not coincided with a hawkish repricing," despite widespread expectations that the central bank is set to raise rates again at its final meeting of the year, on Dec. 9, Allen said.
Today, markets are pricing fewer Fed rate hikes through September 2027 than they were on Oct. 6, when the S&P 500 set its record, Allen said. "If anything, pricing has shifted slightly dovishly with the equity declines."
Over more than six decades since 1962, bear markets have always coincided with at least one of those three circumstances, according to Allen.
"So it would be unusual to see one today without those" happening too, he said.

articles.title_orig: Italians killed in Kuwait: Why is Iran denying responsibility?
articles.title_zh: Italians killed in Kuwait: Why is Iran denying responsibility?
articles.content_orig:
Two Italian technicians have been killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.
The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?
On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.
Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.
The men were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.
They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.
The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.
This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .
Iran said it last struck Kuwait on November 18 .
Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.
After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.
Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.
Iran has denied any involvement.
“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.
Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.
The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.
The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.
Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.
This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.
Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.
“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”
He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”
Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.
As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.
Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.
“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.
Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.
“It’s bizarre to suggest the United States would coordinate this attack on Kuwait, an ally in the Gulf, just to stir up feelings,” he said.
Von Schirach noted that Italy has refused to join the US war on Iran and does not support it. “Italy isn’t on America’s side in this conflict,” he said. “So we shouldn’t take this seriously.”
Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said it was important to “separate Iranian-made from Iranian-launched and Iranian-ordered”.
Tajani described the drone as Iranian-built, of a type also used by Iran-backed militias. Seloom said that makes an Iraqi armed faction the leading alternative suspect. Such groups have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the war began.
He called Yemen’s Houthis “a distant second” and said Tehran’s own suspects, the US, Israel and Ukraine, “come with no evidence”.
“Only debris, radar tracks and a launch point can settle it,” he told Al Jazeera.
Iran’s “false-flag” defence is not new.
Seloom said Tehran first used it in March over strikes on Turkiye, Cyprus and Azerbaijan . However, he said that The Soufan Center, a US-based security think tank, found that it failed to convince Baku.
Claims have run the other way, too. The best known was the reported arrest of Mossad agents plotting bombings in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which came to nothing, Seloom said, because neither of those governments stood behind it.
“Alleged often, verified never, as far as I can establish,” he said. “What this war has is deniable action. Hiding the author is common. Framing someone else has yet to be shown.”
In the case of Thursday’s attack, he said, Iran’s false-flag claim “stands without evidence so far”.
Abdullah al-Shayji, a professor of political science at Kuwait University, said Iran’s narrative “doesn’t come close to being rational or acceptable”.
“Iran bombed us eight days ago, on the 18th of this month, and didn’t deny it,” he said. He said Iran had fired 925 missiles and drones at Kuwait since the start of the war, and more projectiles at Gulf states and Jordan than at Israel. “This doesn’t fool anyone,” he said.
Al-Shayji said the denial comes down to who was killed and where. “Italian technicians were killed, and not at a US base,” he said.
That undermines Iran’s longstanding argument that it hits only US military targets, he said, an argument he believes

articles.title_orig: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
articles.title_zh: Grace Tame: Ex-media executive admits saying child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
articles.content_orig:
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

articles.title_orig: German sofware giant SAP weighs at least 10,000 job cuts amid AI shift, reports say
articles.title_zh: German sofware giant SAP weighs at least 10,000 job cuts amid AI shift, reports say
articles.content_orig:
SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter.
"The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC.
"As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation."
The company did not provide any further details on potential job cuts.
The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."
"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.
"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."
Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.
Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.
In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.
The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.
Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.
In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.
The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy . This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.
The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

articles.title_orig: The last days of Labour Britain
articles.title_zh: The last days of Labour Britain
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Britain will be granted "Swiss-style" consultation rights over European Union legislation but no decision-making powers under agrifood and emissions trading deals agreed at last week’s U.K.-EU summit.
The details were set out in legal texts published on Thursday ahead of the introduction to parliament of the government’s ‘Cutting Costs’ (European Partnership) Bill, the legislation being used to implement the agreements.
The agrifood deal will see the U.K. align with most EU sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules, removing the need for costly border controls. The emissions trading system (ETS) deal will reconnect U.K. and EU carbon markets, shielding businesses on both sides from paying carbon taxes.
Both deals allow the U.K. to be consulted on relevant EU legislative proposals and to contribute views during the drafting process, including through expert discussions and committee meetings. However, the U.K. will have no vote or formal role in EU decision-making.
French negotiators had initially resisted the consultative powers set out in the deals, before ultimately backing down on the eve of the summit.
Joël Reland, a senior research fellow at UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said the U.K.’s role would be akin to Switzerland, which can participate in early legislative consultation phases and still has to actively apply legislation itself.
This will give parliament “some notional power to resist,” Reland explained, “though with the size of Labour's majority we're unlikely to see any obstruction in the near future.”
This model diverges from that of the Windsor Framework, a U.K.-EU deal that controls the flow of goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, where Northern Ireland has no say over the legislation, which is applied by default.
While the U.K. will not be afforded all the rights of an EU member country, Adam Berman, director of policy and advocacy at Energy UK, said it was “positive to see an openness to the U.K. as a decision-shaper” in the ETS deal.
“This should benefit both sides given that the U.K. has substantial expertise in this area,” he added.
In the case of the agrifood deal, the legal text confirms exceptions to alignment on the export of live animals, pet smuggling and precision-bred plants, as well as transitional arrangements for novel foods, pesticides and organic products. These details were set out in an explanatory document published by the U.K. government last week.
The legal text also confirms reports of a 10-year termination clause in the agrifood deal, which requires either side to pay “reasonable and proportionate” costs to rebuild border infrastructure if the deal is scrapped.
Meanwhile, the text of the ETS deal confirms that the U.K. will have freedom to use its Emissions Trading System to reward high-emitting industries which integrate greenhouse gas removal technologies into their manufacturing processes.
The U.K. will keep all revenue drawn from its emissions trading scheme and retain autonomy over how it is spent.
The U.K. will be required to pay both an “operational contribution” towards the EU’s food security system, as well as an additional “participation fee,” calculated at 4% of the operational contribution.

articles.title_orig: Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
articles.title_zh: Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites in space for the creation of data centers critical to powering artificial intelligence.
The decision comes as the US races to lead the world in AI, a technology that promises to turbocharge innovation and economic growth. Harnessing AI is also central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company cautioned in a regulatory filing ahead of its June initial public offering that launching data centers in space relied on “unproven” technologies and “may not achieve commercial viability.”
Deploying SpaceX’s “Starmind” constellation – comprised of 1 million orbital compute modules – will help meet “rapidly growing demand” for AI computing power, the FCC said in a statement Wednesday. The deployed satellites will “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the agency added.
“This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
AI data centers require enormous amounts of energy and Musk has endorsed orbital data centers that can harness the power of the sun.
“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost ​and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX ​told the FCC when it applied for permission to launch the satellites earlier this year.
Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X, his social media platform, that “this will be a great asset to America and the world.”
The initiative has drawn criticism from the scientific community, however, who have argued that the technology could disrupt views of the night sky and increase pollution. In a statement Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society said it was “dismayed” by the FCC’s decision, which it had opposed in earlier filings to the agency.
The “proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the organization said.
It noted that the satellites would be visible as “extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky” and would generate “radio emissions” and “waste heat” that would “threaten… sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research.” It also warned of “atmospheric pollution” from the launches and reentries so many satellites.
Under the license, SpaceX must deploy at least one authorized space station by November 2033, deploy 10% of the total – or 100,000 – by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038.
There are currently around 16,700 operational satellites in space, according to Orbital Radar , a platform providing real-time tracking of objects in orbit. The European Space Agency puts the number of functioning satellites slightly lower, at 15,800.
Earlier this month, in a historic test flight , SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft deployed Starlink internet satellites before returning to earth and pulling of an unprecedented landing.
